items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: The interviewee discusses the structural differences between his 14-piece band and Louis Armstrong's smaller bands which featured Buster Bailey, but does not state any personal interaction or professional collaboration with Buster Bailey himself.

ctx.x: So for instance, there never was one individual that stood out and the whole number built around him. It was a band. And it featured everyone in the band that could play.

But you go to, you used to go to Louis Armstrong concerts, say in the 50s and the 60s. And he would then, he'd have one number, like he'd have a program built in such a way that he'd feature Buster Bailey on Memphis Blue. But that was a later thing. You never had a star deal.

Yeah, but here's the difference here. There was only five or six pieces there. Mine, I had 14. So you couldn't combine it to one individual. But five piece bands, yes, that's how they had to operate. Well, for instance, the concert last night, it would have been lost if you couldn't feature each individual.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-05-11
items.q: Then you had Buster Bailey and guys like that in those days. They failed to mention. And all those guys were great, great musicians.

ctx.x: And not very many people have mentioned him in the books or articles.

That's right. The same way with Mr. Morad. Now there's a few others. There was a great alto player in Dallas, Texas that played on the same style then that Johnny Hodges plays today. His name is Fred Murphy. Fred Murphy. That's right. Now nobody, they failed to mention him. Then you had Buster Bailey and guys like that in those days. They failed to mention. And all those guys were great, great musicians.
Well is Buster from around here?
